Did you know that you can rename VMK adapters on an ESX host relatively easily? Did you know that you can rename VMK adapters on an ESX host relatively easily?
Preparation The ESX host should be in maintenance mode, and a reboot is required to apply the settings. In addition, SSH must be temporarily enabled on the host. You can use esxcfg-vmknic -l to display all vmk adapters on the ESX host.
esxcfg-vmknic -l vmk0 20 IPv4 10.40.13.21 255.255.255.0 10.40.13.255 00:50:56:8e:73:88 1500 65535 true STATIC defaultTcpipStack vmk0 20 IPv6 fe80::250:56ff:fe8e:7388 64 00:50:56:8e:73:88 1500 65535 true STATIC, PREFERRED defaultTcpipStack vmk2 9 IPv4 10.49.50.46 255.255.255.0 10.49.50.255 00:50:56:6b:c1:45 8900 65535 true STATIC defaultTcpipStack vmk2 9 IPv6 fe80::250:56ff:fe6b:c145 64 00:50:56:6b:c1:45 8900 65535 true STATIC, PREFERRED defaultTcpipStack vmk10 5411cfdf-5a53-48be-a593-3fc4614eb396 IPv4 10.40.16.32 255.255.255.0 10.40.16.255 00:50:56:66:da:53 8900 65535 true STATIC vxlan vmk10 5411cfdf-5a53-48be-a593-3fc4614eb396 IPv6 fe80::250:56ff:fe66:da53 64 00:50:56:66:da:53 8900 65535 true STATIC, PREFERRED vxlan vmk11 496dd497-1942-4cb4-a342-32dda43d7b48 IPv4 10.40.16.33 255.255.255.0 10.40.16.255 00:50:56:64:b9:1b 8900 65535 true STATIC vxlan vmk11 496dd497-1942-4cb4-a342-32dda43d7b48 IPv6 fe80::250:56ff:fe64:b91b 64 00:50:56:64:b9:1b 8900 65535 true STATIC, PREFERRED vxlan vmk50 37f1293e-2490-4434-a3c4-e2d2ce975c14 IPv4 169.254.1.1 255.255.0.0 169.254.255.255 00:50:56:63:84:0a 1500 65535 true STATIC hyperbus vmk50 37f1293e-2490-4434-a3c4-e2d2ce975c14 IPv6 fe80::250:56ff:fe63:840a 64 00:50:56:63:84:0a 1500 65535 true STATIC, PREFERRED hyperbus vmk1 1 IPv4 10.40.15.16 255.255.255.0 10.40.15.255 00:50:56:64:5c:8d 8900 65535 true STATIC vmotion vmk1 1 IPv6 fe80::250:56ff:fe64:5c8d 64 00:50:56:64:5c:8d 8900 65535 true STATIC, PREFERRED vmotion Execution First, we export the current configuration of the vmk adapters to a JSON file so we can edit it manually. Then we overwrite the existing configuration with our changes and reboot the system. The changes will then be persistent.
configstorecli config current get -c esx -g network -k vmknics > vmknics.json vi vmknics.json configstorecli config current set -c esx -g network -k vmknics -j vmknics.json --overwrite reboot now Here is a sample JSON from one of my lab hosts.
[ { "device": "vmk0", "dhcp_bound": false, "enabled": true, "enabled_services": { "management": true }, "ip": { "dhcp": false, "dhcp_dns": false, "ipv4_address": "10.40.13.21", "ipv4_subnet_mask": "255.255.255.0", "ipv6": { "auto_configuration_enabled": true, "dhcp": false, "dhcp_dns": false }, "ipv6_enabled": true }, "ip_route_default_gateway": "10.40.13.1", "mac": "00:50:56:8e:73:88", "mac_mode": "PNIC_BASED", "net_stack_instance_key": "defaultTcpipStack", "nic": "vmnic0", "port_connection_type": "VDS", "tso_mss": 0, "vds_port": { "connection_cookie": 953678596, "port_key": "20", "portgroup_name": "wld-cls-vds-01-pg-mgmt", "switch_name": "wld-cls-vds-01", "switch_uuid": "50 01 26 d0 65 60 d8 d9-c6 05 02 f5 c2 49 45 e6" } }, { "device": "vmk1", "enabled": true, "enabled_services": { "vmotion": true }, "ip": { "dhcp": false, "dhcp_dns": false, "ipv4_address": "10.40.15.16", "ipv4_subnet_mask": "255.255.255.0", "ipv6": { "auto_configuration_enabled": false, "dhcp": false, "dhcp_dns": false }, "ipv6_enabled": true }, "ip_route_default_gateway": "0.0.0.0", "mac": "00:50:56:64:5c:8d", "mac_mode": "AUTO_GENERATED", "mtu": 8900, "net_stack_instance_key": "vmotion", "port_connection_type": "VDS", "tso_mss": 0, "vds_port": { "connection_cookie": 949927750, "port_key": "1", "portgroup_name": "wld-cls-vds-01-pg-vmotion", "switch_name": "wld-cls-vds-01", "switch_uuid": "50 01 26 d0 65 60 d8 d9-c6 05 02 f5 c2 49 45 e6" } }, { "device": "vmk2", "enabled": true, "ip": { "dhcp": false, "dhcp_dns": false, "ipv4_address": "10.49.50.46", "ipv4_subnet_mask": "255.255.255.0", "ipv6": { "auto_configuration_enabled": false, "dhcp": false, "dhcp_dns": false }, "ipv6_enabled": true }, "ip_route_default_gateway": "10.49.50.1", "mac": "00:50:56:6b:c1:45", "mac_mode": "AUTO_GENERATED", "mtu": 8900, "net_stack_instance_key": "defaultTcpipStack", "port_connection_type": "VDS", "tso_mss": 0, "vds_port": { "connection_cookie": 952629631, "port_key": "9", "portgroup_name": "wld-cls-vds-01-pg-nfs", "switch_name": "wld-cls-vds-01", "switch_uuid": "50 01 26 d0 65 60 d8 d9-c6 05 02 f5 c2 49 45 e6" } } ] For demonstration purposes, I renamed my vmk0 to vmk4. (The CLI output has been shortened.)
[root@esxwld01:~] esxcfg-vmknic -l Interface Port Group/DVPort/Opaque Network IP Family IP Address Netmask Broadcast MAC Address MTU TSO MSS Enabled Type NetStack vmk4 20 IPv4 10.40.13.21 255.255.255.0 10.40.13.255 00:50:56:8e:73:88 1500 65535 true STATIC defaultTcpipStack vmk4 20 IPv6 fe80::250:56ff:fe8e:7388 64 00:50:56:8e:73:88 1500 65535 true STATIC, PREFERRED defaultTcpipStack Why? Well, the answer is relatively simple: to simplify operation and troubleshooting. When you build a VCF cluster with different network configurations (different server generations or more network cards), it can be confusing when you try to troubleshoot something in the logs and find that the vMotion VMK adapter is adapter 2 on one server and adapter 3 on another. Another example is Host Add in a VxRail VCF cluster. With VCF 9.1, the VxRail host loses its VMK 0 discovery interface after host commissioning. As a result, the VMK assignment no longer matches that of the existing host. This isn’t really a problem, but having identical VMK names makes operations easier.
A quick warning to wrap things upDo not use this method to change the names of the NSX vmk adapters!
title: Renaming vmk Adapter
